title: Alcohol Withdrawal After Surgery
sub: Post-op day 1, ankle ORIF · Orthopedic unit
profile: 52-year-old man, postoperative day 1 after ankle ORIF following a fall. He initially reported weekend drinking; with consent, partner clarifies daily heavy drinking and last drink 36 hours before current assessment, plus a documented prior withdrawal seizure. Now restless/diaphoretic with hand tremor, visual/tactile hallucinations, HR 118/min, BP 166/98 mmHg, SpO₂ 96% on room air; incision clean, pedal pulse 2+, pain 4/10. At initial assessment he remains oriented and can answer CIWA-Ar questions reliably; score 18, magnesium 1.3 mg/dL, MCV 104 fL, AST 96 U/L, ALT 40 U/L. Prescribed symptom-triggered lorazepam, prompt thiamine, magnesium replacement and seizure/respiratory precautions. If delirium prevents reliable responses, use the facility’s appropriate observational assessment rather than CIWA-Ar. Treat any hypoglycemia promptly without waiting for thiamine.

Notes: Nurses' notes 21:30 (post-op day 1)

Client restless and picking at the bed sheets. States, "There are bugs crawling all over this bed." Hands tremble when he reaches for his water cup. Skin diaphoretic. Oriented to person and place but not to time. Right ankle incision clean, dry and intact; pedal pulse 2+ with brisk capillary refill. Rates ankle pain 4/10. Voided 350 mL clear yellow urine.
Family report 21:45

Spouse states the client drinks about a fifth (750 mL) of vodka every day. His last drink was at about 09:00 yesterday, shortly before the fall (about 36 hours ago). Last year he had "a shaking fit and passed out" when he tried to stop drinking on his own.
Nurses' notes 21:50
CIWA-Ar completed: score 18. Provider notified; new orders received.
Vitals: BP 166/98 mm Hg · HR 118 (sinus tachycardia) · RR 22 · SpO₂ 96% on room air · T 37.9 °C (100.2 °F)
BP 138/84 mm Hg · HR 92 · RR 18 · SpO₂ 97% on room air · T 37.1 °C (98.8 °F)
Labs: Na⁺ 136 mEq/L · K⁺ 3.4 mEq/L · Magnesium 1.3 mg/dL (normal 1.7–2.2) · Glucose 84 mg/dL · AST 118 U/L · ALT 52 U/L · MCV 104 fL (normal 80–100) · Platelets 118,000/mm³ · Hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL
Orders: Active
Oxycodone 5 mg PO every 4 hours PRN moderate pain · Lactated Ringer's at 75 mL/hr · Elevate right leg · Non-weight-bearing right leg

CIWA-Ar every hour while the score is 10 or higher, then every 4 hours · Lorazepam IV per symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar protocol, as prescribed · Thiamine 100 mg IV now, then daily · Folic acid 1 mg PO daily · Multivitamin PO daily · Magnesium sulfate IV as prescribed · Change IV fluid to dextrose 5% in 0.45% sodium chloride at 75 mL/hr · Seizure precautions · Notify provider for CIWA-Ar above 20 or any seizure

items.stem: Tap the findings in the record that suggest the client is withdrawing from alcohol.
passage: Restless, picking at the bed sheets
States bugs are crawling on the bed
Hands tremble when reaching for a cup
items.rationale: Stopping alcohol after heavy daily use removes its depressant effect on the brain, so the nervous system becomes overactive. That shows up as tremor, sweating, a fast heart rate, high blood pressure, restlessness, and tactile or visual hallucinations such as "bugs on the bed." The incision and pedal pulse are normal, pain of 4/10 is expected and controlled the day after ankle surgery, and an SpO₂ of 96% is normal.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: The client's findings are most consistent with
and his CIWA-Ar score of 18 indicates
opts: minimal withdrawal that needs only monitoring
a score that is not valid after surgery

blanks.pre: and his high MCV with an AST more than twice his ALT points to

items.rationale: Timing and collateral history support withdrawal. CIWA-Ar 18 is moderate by ASAM and warrants protocol-directed treatment in a reliably communicative client; it does not independently classify severe withdrawal. Hypomagnesemia raises concern and needs replacement. Macrocytosis and AST-predominant elevation can support the history but are nonspecific and not proof of alcohol use. If delirium compromises self-report, use an appropriate observational scale.

items.stem: About 36 hours after his last drink, the client is at highest immediate risk for which complication?
options: Withdrawal seizures with progression to delirium tremens
Hepatic encephalopathy from alcohol-related liver disease
Fat embolism syndrome from the ankle fracture
Respiratory depression from the PRN oxycodone
items.rationale: Prior withdrawal seizure, current symptoms and 36-hour cessation make seizure prevention and close surveillance urgent. Withdrawal seizures and delirium are possible complications, not an inevitable serial progression. The displayed pattern does not establish hepatic encephalopathy, fat embolism or current opioid hypoventilation; assess alternative causes when the clinical course suggests them.

items.stem: For each intervention, mark whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client now.
rows: Keep the bed low with padded side rails up, and keep suction and oxygen at the bedside
Give lorazepam according to the CIWA-Ar score
Start the dextrose 5% IV fluid before giving the first dose of thiamine
Keep the room quiet and well lit, and reorient him often
Apply bilateral wrist restraints so he cannot pull out his IV
Hold all lorazepam doses because he also has an order for oxycodone
items.rationale: Use seizure precautions, prescribed benzodiazepine treatment, calm reorientation and prompt thiamine. ASAM allows glucose/thiamine in either order or concurrently; never delay urgent glucose for thiamine. Do not apply restraints automatically; use assessed least-restrictive measures. The opioid order requires careful sedation/respiratory review rather than automatic omission of all withdrawal treatment. Hold unsafe sedating doses and escalate when respiratory compromise occurs.

items.stem: At 23:10, the client has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Turn the client onto his side
Note the time the seizure starts and how long it lasts
Cushion his head and move nearby objects away
Insert an oral airway between his teeth
Hold his arms and legs to stop the jerking
Leave the room to bring the emergency cart
items.rationale: A side-lying position lets saliva drain and keeps the tongue from blocking the airway. Timing the seizure guides treatment and must be reported. Cushioning the head and clearing the area prevent injury. An IV benzodiazepine treats the seizure and the withdrawal that caused it. Forcing anything between the teeth can break teeth or cause aspiration. Restraining the limbs can cause fractures and does not stop the seizure. The nurse stays with the client and uses the call light to summon help.

items.stem: The client has received thiamine, IV magnesium and several lorazepam doses overnight. For each finding, mark whether it shows improvement or requires follow-up.
rows: No further seizure activity during the night
05:30: after PRN oxycodone, opens eyes only to a loud voice; RR 10
items.rationale: Lower reliable CIWA scores/vital signs, no recurrent seizures and corrected magnesium are favorable. Difficulty arousing with RR 10 after combined sedatives requires immediate airway/ventilation assessment, withholding further sedatives and calling for help. Support ventilation and give cause-appropriate ordered reversal when indicated; monitoring/notification alone must not delay rescue. Continue withdrawal surveillance using an appropriate assessment tool.

title: Lithium Toxicity
sub: Dehydration and a new NSAID · Emergency department
profile: 34-year-old woman with bipolarI disorder taking lithium carbonate for 3 years. Partner reports prescribed dosing without extra doses and steady mood. Recent vomiting/diarrhea, poor intake and ibuprofen use for wrist pain. Baseline creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, now 1.6 mg/dL; lithium 2.4 mEq/L, glucose 96 mg/dL, TSH within lab range. Coarse tremor, twitching, slurred speech, orientation to person only and ataxic gait; BP 98/60 mmHg, HR 112/min, SpO₂ 97%. ECG shows flattened T waves. Hold lithium/NSAIDs, give prescribed reassessed isotonic fluid and monitor neurologic/cardiac/renal status. Urgent toxicology/poison-center and nephrology consultation evaluate significant confusion, renal dysfunction, serial levels and dialysis indications; hydration alone is not assumed sufficient.

Notes: Triage 14:20

Partner reports 3 days of vomiting and watery diarrhea after a "stomach bug," with very little to eat or drink. Five days ago the client started over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours for a sprained wrist. Partner fills her weekly pill organizer and confirms she has taken lithium only as prescribed. Partner states her mood has been "steady for months."
Nurses' notes 14:35

Client drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only. Speech slurred. Coarse tremor of both hands; muscle twitching noted in both arms. Unsteady, wide-based gait; needed two-person assist to the stretcher. Mucous membranes dry. Denies thoughts of self-harm. No muscle rigidity.
Vitals: BP 98/60 mm Hg · HR 112 (sinus tachycardia, flattened T waves) · RR 18 · SpO₂ 97% on room air · T 37.2 °C (99.0 °F)
Labs: Lithium 2.4 mEq/L (therapeutic 0.6–1.2) · Na⁺ 132 mEq/L · K⁺ 3.4 mEq/L · BUN 38 mg/dL · Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL · Glucose 96 mg/dL · Urine specific gravity 1.030
Lithium 0.9 mEq/L · Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL · TSH 2.1 mIU/L
Orders: ED standing order set
Ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 6 hours PRN moderate pain · Ondansetron 4 mg IV every 6 hours PRN nausea

Hold lithium · 0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL IV bolus, then 150 mL/hr · Repeat lithium level and basic metabolic panel in 4 hours · Continuous cardiac monitoring · Seizure and fall precautions · Strict intake and output · Nephrology consult regarding hemodialysis

items.stem: Which findings require immediate follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
options: Coarse hand tremor and muscle twitching
Slurred speech and orientation to person only
Partner reports her mood has been steady
items.rationale: Elevated lithium with neurologic findings, creatinine doubling and abnormal hemodynamics needs urgent toxicity/renal/volume assessment. Severity depends on symptoms, chronicity and renal clearance, not level alone. The displayed stable mood, glucose and saturation do not remove the toxicity emergency; significant confusion requires specialist consideration of extracorporeal treatment.

items.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the rise in the client's lithium level?
options: Fluid and sodium losses plus ibuprofen reduced how much lithium her kidneys excrete
She took extra lithium doses because her bipolar symptoms returned
Hypothyroidism slowed the liver's breakdown of lithium
Vomiting concentrated the lithium already in her stomach
items.rationale: Lithium is excreted almost entirely by the kidneys, which handle it much like sodium. When a client loses fluid and sodium, the kidneys hold on to sodium and reabsorb lithium with it. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen also reduce kidney blood flow and lithium clearance. Her partner confirms she took doses as prescribed and her mood is stable. Lithium is not broken down by the liver, and her TSH was normal. Vomiting removes drug from the stomach rather than concentrating it.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Give IV 0.9% sodium chloride as prescribed
Restrict oral fluids to 1 liter per day
Give the next lithium dose with food
Request IV haloperidol for her confusion
Level of consciousness, tremor and gait

items.rationale: Hold lithium and give the prescribed carefully reassessed isotonic fluid while urgently involving toxicology/nephrology. Monitor serial lithium/renal results and neurologic course; significant confusion and impaired clearance require dialysis consideration under EXTRIP rather than hydration-only management. Fluid restriction/another lithium dose is inappropriate here; a nonspecific antipsychotic request does not correct the toxic exposure.

items.stem: For each intervention, mark whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client.
rows: Place the client on continuous cardiac monitoring
Keep the bed low and assist with all movement
Provide a low-sodium diet once she can eat
Keep strict intake and output records
Encourage her to walk the hallway to reduce muscle twitching
items.rationale: Lithium toxicity can cause dysrhythmias, so continuous monitoring is needed (her ECG already shows flattened T waves). Ataxia and confusion put her at high risk for falls, and severe toxicity can cause seizures. Close intake and output tracking shows whether fluids are restoring kidney function. Activated charcoal does not bind lithium. A low-sodium diet makes the kidneys reabsorb more lithium. Walking an ataxic, confused client is unsafe and does not treat the twitching.

items.stem: While the saline bolus infuses, the client asks for something for her wrist pain, which she rates 5/10. The ED standing order set includes ibuprofen 400 mg PO PRN. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Withhold the ibuprofen and ask the provider for a non-NSAID analgesic
Give the ibuprofen with food to protect her stomach
Give half the ibuprofen dose because of her kidney function
Tell her no pain medicine can be given until her lithium level is normal
items.rationale: NSAIDs decrease lithium clearance and helped cause this toxicity, and her kidneys are already injured. The nurse withholds the drug and contacts the provider for a safer choice, such as acetaminophen if prescribed. Food protects the stomach but does not change the effect on lithium. A smaller NSAID dose still reduces kidney blood flow. Leaving her pain untreated is not necessary because safer options exist.

items.stem: Two days later her lithium level is 0.8 mEq/L and her creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Before discharge, the nurse reviews teaching. For each statement by the client, mark whether it shows understanding or needs more teaching.
rows: "I'll drink 2 to 3 liters of fluid a day, and more when it's hot or I'm sweating."
"If I get vomiting or diarrhea again, I'll call my provider about my lithium."
"Next time my wrist hurts, I'll take naproxen instead of ibuprofen."
"I should cut back on salt as much as I can to protect my kidneys."
"If my hand shaking gets worse or I feel confused or unsteady, I'll get help right away."
"I'll have my lithium level drawn about 12 hours after my last dose."
items.rationale: Steady fluid intake, extra fluid with heat or sweating, and calling the provider during vomiting or diarrhea prevent dehydration-related toxicity. Worsening tremor, confusion or an unsteady gait are early warning signs. Lithium levels are drawn as a trough, about 12 hours after the last dose. Naproxen is also an NSAID and raises lithium levels the same way. Sodium intake should stay normal and consistent; a low-salt diet causes the kidneys to keep more lithium.

title: Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression on a PCA
sub: Post-op night 1, open colectomy · Surgical unit
profile: 71-year-old woman with OSA/homeCPAP and BMI 36, opioid-naive before open hemicolectomy, postoperative night 1. HomeCPAP unavailable. MAR/PCA:hydromorphone 0.2 mg demand dose,10-minute lockout, no basal infusion; diphenhydramine 25 mg given at 01:30. Daughter reports pressing the PCA during sleep at 02:00–03:30; ondansetron was ordered but not administered. At 03:40 responds only to firm stimulation, RR 6/shallow with pauses 15 seconds, pupils 2 mm/equal, SpO₂ 86% on 2 L/min, ETCO₂ 62 mmHg, palpable pulse 68/min, BP 118/70, temperature 36.8°C, glucose 118 mg/dL, dry dressing. Stop PCA, activate resuscitation assistance, continuously monitor and immediately assist ventilation. Prescribed postoperative naloxone titration 0.04 mg IV with reassessment every 2 minutes/repeat as needed to adequate ventilation and arousability; stocked 0.4 mg/mL solution. Preparation must not delay ventilation or available reversal.

Notes: Nurses' notes 23:00
Awake, oriented, rates abdominal pain 5/10. Using the hydromorphone PCA correctly. Pasero Opioid-Induced Sedation Scale (POSS) 2. Daughter staying overnight.
Nurses' notes 03:40

Client difficult to arouse; moans and briefly opens her eyes to a firm sternal rub, then falls back asleep without answering questions. Loud snoring respirations with pauses up to 15 seconds. Pupils 2 mm, equal and reactive. Skin cool and dry. Abdominal dressing dry and intact. Daughter states, "I kept pushing her button whenever she moaned so she wouldn't wake up in pain." POSS 4.
Vitals: BP 108/62 mm Hg · HR 58 · RR 6, shallow · SpO₂ 86% on 2 L nasal cannula · ETCO₂ 62 mm Hg · T 36.8 °C (98.2 °F)
BP 132/78 mm Hg · HR 84 · RR 16 · SpO₂ 95% on 2 L nasal cannula · ETCO₂ 38 mm Hg
Labs: Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL · Na⁺ 139 mEq/L · K⁺ 4.0 mEq/L · Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL · Glucose 118 mg/dL
MAR: Hydromorphone: 26 demand attempts, 18 doses delivered (3.6 mg total)
Diphenhydramine 25 mg IV given for itching
Orders: Active

Hydromorphone PCA: demand dose 0.2 mg, lockout 10 minutes, no basal rate · Continuous pulse oximetry and capnography · Oxygen 2 L/min by nasal cannula · Diphenhydramine 25 mg IV every 6 hours PRN itching · Ondansetron 4 mg IV every 6 hours PRN nausea
Opioid reversal protocol

For RR below 8 or POSS 4: stop the opioid, call the rapid response team, and give naloxone 0.4 mg diluted in 9 mL 0.9% sodium chloride (0.04 mg/mL), 0.04 mg IV every 2 minutes until RR is 10 or more and the client opens her eyes to voice

items.stem: Tap the findings at 03:40 that are consistent with opioid toxicity.
passage: Responds only to a firm sternal rub
items.rationale: Sedation so deep that only a sternal rub gets a response, slow shallow breathing with long pauses, pinpoint pupils, low oxygen saturation and a high end-tidal CO₂ (normal 35–45 mm Hg) are the pattern of opioid toxicity with respiratory depression. The dry dressing, normal temperature and mildly raised post-op glucose are not caused by the opioid and do not need urgent action.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: The client's findings are most consistent with
and the rise in ETCO₂ shows she is
opts: retaining carbon dioxide because she is hypoventilating
breathing off too much carbon dioxide
getting enough ventilation from her oxygen
blanks.answer: retaining carbon dioxide because she is hypoventilating

blanks.pre: Her risk was raised by sleep apnea, being opioid-naive, the recent diphenhydramine and
opts: PCA doses her daughter gave while she slept
blanks.answer: PCA doses her daughter gave while she slept

items.rationale: The supplied MAR/family report identifies opioid plus sedating-antihistamine exposure and PCA by proxy in an OSA/opioid-naive client. Rising ETCO₂ reflects inadequate ventilation; oxygen alone cannot remove retainedCO₂. Only the capable client may press a self-administered PCA button. Safety also depends on selection, settings and monitoring; a lockout does not make family administration safe. Other causes remain assessed clinically rather than excluded by one finding.

items.stem: Which problem is the nurse's priority?
options: Hypoventilation with carbon dioxide retention and hypoxemia
Postoperative pain that may return if the opioid is stopped
Risk for falls related to sedation
items.rationale: Breathing is the immediate threat: an RR of 6 with apneic pauses, an SpO₂ of 86% and a rising ETCO₂ can progress to respiratory arrest. Pain control matters and will be planned for, but it comes after breathing. Infection and falls are potential problems, while hypoventilation is happening now.

items.stem: For each intervention, mark whether it is indicated or not indicated right now.
rows: Open the airway and assist breaths with a bag-valve mask if breathing stays inadequate
Give naloxone 0.4 mg undiluted by rapid IV push
Let her sleep and recheck her in 1 hour
Increase the nasal cannula to 6 L/min as the only intervention
items.rationale: Stop opioid delivery, summon help, open the airway and immediately assist inadequate ventilation while administering prescribed naloxone. Postoperative small-dose titration seeks adequate breathing while limiting abrupt pain reversal, but 0.4 mg is not universally contraindicated for life-threatening overdose. Never withhold rescue while awaiting dilution. Sleeping/rechecking later or oxygen escalation alone does not treat this hypoventilation.

items.stem: Assisted ventilation and continuous monitoring are already underway. The prescribed titration is 0.04 mg IV with reassessment every 2 minutes. Stock naloxone is 0.4 mg/mL. Order the preparation/dose/reassessment actions; rescue continues throughout.
steps: Wait 2 minutes, then reassess her respiratory rate and level of sedation
Dilute naloxone 0.4 mg with 9 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride
Keep monitoring respirations, sedation, SpO₂ and ETCO₂ closely for re-sedation
Give 0.04 mg (1 mL) by slow IV push
Repeat 0.04 mg every 2 minutes until RR is 10 or more and she opens her eyes to voice
items.rationale: 0.4 mg in total 10 mL gives 0.04 mg/mL;1 mL supplies the ordered 0.04 mg dose. Follow each dose with the specified reassessment and conditional repeat/escalation. Ventilation/monitoring begin before and continue during titration. Naloxone can wear off before the opioid; continued observation and an individualized plan prevent missed recurrence. Do not postpone urgent available rescue for custom preparation.

items.stem: She received a total of 0.12 mg of naloxone. For each finding, mark whether it is an expected response or requires follow-up.
rows: 04:10: RR 14, opens her eyes when spoken to, POSS 2
04:10: SpO₂ 95% on 2 L, ETCO₂ 44 mm Hg
04:10: rates abdominal pain 5/10 and says, "I can manage it"
04:15: daughter asks if she can go back to pressing the PCA button for her mother
05:20: POSS 3, drifts off to sleep mid-sentence, RR 9
items.rationale: Improved ventilation/arousability, oxygenation/ETCO₂ and manageable pain are favorable. PCA-by-proxy teaching is required. Recurrent POSS 3 with RR 9 needs immediate respiratory assessment, continued opioid withholding, emergency assistance and ventilation/repeat naloxone under protocol when indicated; it is not a routine later follow-up. Reassess the opioid/OSA monitoring and analgesia plan before any restart.

title: Anaphylaxis During an IV Antibiotic
sub: First dose of cefazolin · Medical unit
profile: 45-year-old man admitted with left-leg cellulitis, no known drug allergies. At 10:00 pre-infusion assessment:BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 90/min, SpO₂ 97% on room air, temperature 38.0°C, WBC 14,200/µL, leg red/warm/swollen; normal voice and no hives/wheezing. First cefazolin infusion begins 10:05. At 10:12 new hoarse voice/throat tightness, lip swelling/generalized hives, expiratory wheezes, BP 84/48, HR 124/min and SpO₂ 89%. Emergency anaphylaxis orders include immediate trigger cessation, IM epinephrine 0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL solution into anterolateral thigh, repeat assessment/dosing per protocol, oxygen/airway support and reassessed isotonic-fluid bolus through suitable new tubing. The resuscitation team performs these actions concurrently; antihistamine is adjunctive after immediate rescue.

Notes: Admission 08:30
Left lower leg red, warm, swollen and tender from ankle to mid-calf; borders marked with a skin pen. No drainage. Lungs clear. Skin otherwise intact without rash.
Nurses' notes 10:12

Client pressed the call light. States, "My throat feels tight and I itch all over. Something bad is happening." Voice hoarse. Raised hives on the chest, back and both arms. Lips and eyelids swelling. Expiratory wheezes in all lung fields. Restless and anxious. Cefazolin infusion running, about 40% infused.
Vitals: BP 84/48 mm Hg · HR 128 (sinus tachycardia) · RR 28 · SpO₂ 89% on room air · T 38.0 °C (100.4 °F)
BP 132/80 mm Hg · HR 96 · RR 18 · SpO₂ 97% on room air · T 38.0 °C (100.4 °F)
Labs: WBC 14,200/mm³ · Hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL · Platelets 260,000/mm³ · Na⁺ 138 mEq/L · K⁺ 4.1 mEq/L · Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · Glucose 104 mg/dL
Orders: Active
Cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours (first dose started 10:00) · 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL/hr · Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN fever · Elevate left leg
Anaphylaxis protocol

Epinephrine 0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) IM into the anterolateral thigh; may repeat every 5–15 minutes · Oxygen by nonrebreather mask to keep SpO₂ 94% or higher · 0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL IV bolus · Diphenhydramine IV as prescribed · Methylprednisolone IV as prescribed · Albuterol nebulizer for persistent wheezing

items.stem: Which findings at 10:12 require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Hives on the chest, back and arms with lip swelling
Expiratory wheezes in all lung fields
Red, warm, swollen left lower leg
items.rationale: Within minutes of starting a new drug, he has developed upper airway swelling (hoarseness, tight throat, lip swelling), widespread hives, bronchospasm (wheezes), low oxygen and a sudden drop in blood pressure. These are new and life-threatening. The red leg, low-grade fever and high WBC were present before the infusion and are explained by the cellulitis being treated.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: The client is having anaphylaxis, in which
opts: mast cells release histamine and other mediators
the antibiotic builds up to a toxic level
bacteria release toxins into the blood
blanks.answer: mast cells release histamine and other mediators

blanks.pre: which explains his hypotension. His hoarseness, wheezing and low SpO₂ are caused by airway swelling and

items.rationale: Anaphylaxis involves mast-cell/basophil mediator release through IgE or non-IgE pathways. Vasodilation/capillary leak causes hypotension and swelling; bronchospasm/airway edema impairs breathing. The abrupt multi-system pattern after cefazolin supports anaphylaxis rather than isolated dose toxicity or cellulitis-related fever. Mechanism is not proven solely from this clinical presentation.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take first, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Give epinephrine IM into the anterolateral thigh
Give oral diphenhydramine and recheck in 30 minutes
Slow the infusion rate and monitor
Airway and breathing: voice, stridor, wheezing and SpO₂
Size of the marked cellulitis border

items.rationale: Hives with airway swelling, wheezing and hypotension minutes after a new IV drug is anaphylaxis. Septic shock would not cause hives and lip swelling, asthma does not cause hypotension and hives, and a vasovagal reaction causes a slow pulse, not tachycardia. Stopping the drug removes the trigger, and IM epinephrine is the first-line drug because it reverses vasodilation, airway swelling and bronchospasm. Antihistamines are add-on drugs that do not treat airway obstruction or shock, slowing the infusion still gives more of the trigger, and acetaminophen does nothing for the reaction. Blood pressure, heart rate and airway and breathing status show whether epinephrine is working and whether another dose is needed.

items.stem: For each intervention, mark whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client.
rows: Position him lying flat with legs raised, or semi-reclining with legs raised if breathing is hard
Flush the IV line to clear the remaining cefazolin into his vein
Bring airway and intubation equipment to the bedside
Help him stand and walk to the bathroom if he asks
Give diphenhydramine instead of epinephrine because the hives are the main problem
Plan to monitor him for several hours for a return of symptoms
items.rationale: Lying flat with the legs raised supports blood return to the heart; a client who is struggling to breathe may semi-recline. Airway swelling can progress quickly, so equipment for an advanced airway must be ready. Flushing the line would push more of the drug into him; the tubing is replaced and the IV access kept. Standing up suddenly during anaphylactic shock can cause cardiovascular collapse. Antihistamines only relieve itching and hives and never replace epinephrine. Symptoms can return hours later (a biphasic reaction), so ongoing observation is needed.

items.stem: The rapid response team has been activated. Which actions should proceed immediately during this anaphylactic emergency? Select all that apply.
steps: Start the 0.9% sodium chloride bolus through new tubing
Give epinephrine 0.5 mg IM into the anterolateral thigh
items.rationale: Remove the trigger and give IM epinephrine immediately while team members support oxygenation/airway and circulation concurrently. Do not impose an oxygen-before-fluid delay in simultaneous hypoxemia/shock. Antihistamine relieves skin symptoms but does not replace epinephrine or treat obstructed airway/shock. Standing risks collapse. Reassess for repeat epinephrine and escalation under protocol.

items.stem: One dose of epinephrine and 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride have been given. For each finding, mark whether it shows improvement or requires follow-up.
rows: 10:30: SpO₂ 96% on nonrebreather; wheezes no longer heard
10:30: voice normal; says his throat no longer feels tight
10:30: hives fading on the chest and arms
15:00: new hives and a hoarse voice; says, "My throat is getting tight again"
items.rationale: A normal blood pressure, good oxygenation, clear lungs, a normal voice and fading hives show the treatment worked. New airway symptoms hours later signal a biphasic reaction, which can occur without re-exposure and can be as severe as the first; the nurse treats it as anaphylaxis again, starting with IM epinephrine per protocol, and calls for help. Cefazolin must also be recorded as an allergy so it is not given again.

title: Delirium After Hip Fracture Repair
profile: 82-year-old woman, postoperative day 2 after left hip hemiarthroplasty. Lives alone, walks with a cane and has no diagnosed dementia; wears glasses/hearing aids. At 16:00 yesterday she was oriented to person/place/time, attentive and CAM negative. At 02:00 now pulls at IV/tries to climb out of bed, oriented only to person, cannot maintain attention or name months backward, fluctuates between drowsiness/agitation, and says she must feed chickens (daughter confirms she owns no chickens). Glasses/hearing aids are in a drawer; diphenhydramine was given for sleep. Last analgesic 14:00 yesterday; self-report is currently unreliable, so local protocol uses a validated observational pain measure (recorded score 5). No stool 4 days; Foley drains without documented retention. Temperature 37.4°C, SpO₂ 94% on room air, incision dry, pulses 2+. Provider evaluates acute delirium and reversible causes; lorazepam has been ordered by phone without a withdrawal indication.

Notes: Nurses' notes yesterday 15:00
Alert and oriented to person, place and time. Conversing appropriately with her daughter. Glasses and hearing aids in use.
Nurses' notes 02:00

Client pulling at her IV and trying to climb out of bed. Calling out for her late husband and says she must "get home to feed the chickens." Oriented to person only. Cannot name the months of the year backward; loses track of the question partway through. Drowsy one minute and agitated the next. Glasses and hearing aids in the bedside drawer. Indwelling urinary catheter in place since surgery. Last bowel movement 4 days ago; abdomen slightly distended. Grimaces and guards her left hip when turned. Incision approximated without drainage; pedal pulses 2+. PAINAD 5. Confusion Assessment Method (CAM): positive.
Vitals: BP 146/82 mm Hg · HR 98 · RR 18 · SpO₂ 94% on room air · T 37.4 °C (99.3 °F)
BP 132/76 mm Hg · HR 84 · RR 16 · SpO₂ 95% on room air · T 37.2 °C (99.0 °F)
Labs: Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL · WBC 9,600/mm³ · Na⁺ 137 mEq/L · K⁺ 4.2 mEq/L · BUN 22 mg/dL · Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · Glucose 112 mg/dL
MAR: Oxycodone 5 mg PO given for hip pain (no further doses requested)
Diphenhydramine 25 mg PO given for sleep
Orders: Active

Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN mild pain · Oxycodone 5 mg PO every 4 hours PRN moderate to severe pain · Diphenhydramine 25 mg PO at bedtime PRN sleep · Out of bed to chair with assistance three times daily; weight-bearing as tolerated · Indwelling urinary catheter to gravity drainage · Enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily
Phone order 02:30
Lorazepam 1 mg IV every 4 hours PRN agitation

items.stem: Tap the findings at 02:00 that show an acute change in the client's mental status.
passage: Pulling at her IV and trying to climb out of bed
Says she must get home to feed the chickens
Drowsy one minute and agitated the next
items.rationale: Yesterday afternoon she was fully oriented. Now she is agitated, disoriented and misperceiving her situation, cannot keep her attention on a simple task, and swings between drowsiness and agitation. The incision, circulation, temperature and oxygen saturation are within expected limits after hip surgery.

items.stem: Which condition best explains the change in the client's mental status?
items.rationale: Delirium starts over hours to days, fluctuates, and is marked by inattention with disorganized thinking or a changing level of consciousness, which is exactly what a positive CAM shows. Dementia develops gradually over months to years, and she was cognitively intact yesterday. Depression causes low mood and slowed thinking, not sudden disorientation and agitation. Confusion is never a normal part of aging; a sudden change always needs to be investigated.

items.stem: Which displayed modifiable factors may contribute to the client’s delirium? Select all that apply.
options: Glasses and hearing aids left in the drawer
Hip pain with a PAINAD score of 5 and no recent analgesia
No bowel movement for 4 days and an indwelling urinary catheter
An order for weight-bearing as tolerated
items.rationale: Anticholinergic diphenhydramine, unavailable sensory aids, inadequately treated pain and constipation/catheter burden are modifiable contributors. The supplied timeline establishes 12 hours since analgesia. Attempt self-report whenever reliable; use the local validated observational tool when it is not. The catheter adds tethering/infection concerns but does not establish retention when it drains. Assess other physiologic/medication causes concurrently. Safe mobility and prescribed thromboprophylaxis are not the displayed causative factors.

items.stem: For each intervention, mark whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client.
rows: Put her glasses and hearing aids back on
Invite her daughter to stay and bring familiar items from home
Ask the provider about removing the urinary catheter and starting a bowel regimen
Assess pain with PAINAD, give analgesia as prescribed, and ask about scheduled acetaminophen
Keep the overhead light and television on all night to help orient her
Apply bilateral soft wrist restraints to protect her IV
items.rationale: Restore sensory aids, use familiar support/reorientation, review catheter need and constipation, assess/treat pain appropriately and investigate reversible causes. Self-report remains preferred when feasible; use a suitable observational tool when unreliable. Preserve sleep with low nighttime noise/light and safe daytime activity. Do not apply automatic restraints to protect an IV; assessed least-restrictive measures come first.

items.stem: At 03:00, the client is calmer with her daughter at the bedside and her glasses and hearing aids in place. Which action should the nurse take about the lorazepam phone order?
options: Contact the provider to discuss the order and ask for a review of her sedating medications
Give the lorazepam now so that she sleeps for the rest of the night
Give the lorazepam if she tries to pull at her IV again
Give half the dose because of her age
items.rationale: The AGS Beers Criteria advise avoiding benzodiazepines in older adults: they can cause or worsen delirium, excess sedation and falls, and they are not used for delirium except in special cases such as alcohol withdrawal. The nurse has a duty to question an order that may harm the client, and should share that nonpharmacologic measures are working and ask about stopping the diphenhydramine. Giving the drug now or at the next sign of agitation exposes her to the same harm, and a nurse cannot change a prescribed dose on their own.

items.stem: Two days later, the nurse reviews the client's progress. For each finding, mark whether it shows improvement or requires follow-up.
rows: 10:00: oriented to person, place and time; CAM negative
Slept about 5 hours last night with the room dark and quiet
Catheter removed; voiding without difficulty; had a bowel movement yesterday
Walked to the chair with a walker and one assist; PAINAD 1
20:00: again does not know where she is and tries to get out of bed without calling
items.rationale: Recovered attention/orientation with negative CAM, sleep, normal elimination, assisted mobility and reliable low pain self-report are favorable findings. Prefer self-report when the client can provide it; an observational score is not interchangeable with a numerical self-report. Delirium can fluctuate, and renewed disorientation/unsafe attempts to rise at 20:00 require immediate safety measures, reassessment of reversible causes and provider follow-up.
